ntrl-demo · rectangle car in (x, y, θ) · 2026-10-30 and 31

Parking Thin-Wall Test

ntrl-demo solves the bay-to-bay move at every divider thickness tried, from 0.30 down to 0.001: 296–300 of 300 runs per training seed. Thinning the divider does not test the field's sharpness here, because in configuration space the car's 0.13 width is added to the wall. Thinning the wall the field actually has to resolve does: each trained field falls to half success at a C-space wall between 0.047 and 0.022, and every one fails at 0.015. Narrowing the free space instead, by widening the car in fixed bays, breaks it at a side gap of about 0.022–0.031, long before the bays demand a steep slope. In both tests the same planner driven by the true travel time solves 299–300 of 300 runs.

The scene

A 0.30 × 0.13 rectangle car parks nose-in in bay A and has to reach bay B: back out (−x), move down (−y), drive in (+x). The lot is the unit square, about 3.3 car lengths a side, closed by outer walls. The divider between the two bays is the wall that gets thinner. Every query is a parked pose in one bay to a parked pose in the other (50 A→B, 50 B→A), certified by a collision-free witness path.

Thinning the divider

With the full-width car, ntrl-demo's metric package (what the demo trains its 2-D maze and 3-D Gibson scenes with) solved 296–300 of the 300 bay-to-bay runs per training seed at every divider from 0.30 to 0.001, with three training seeds for the ten main dividers. The straight segment between the parked poses crosses the divider in every query, so every one of those runs drives around. The demo's arm package, metric_arm, whose input features are five times lower in frequency, is the exception: with one training seed it solves 198 of 300 at the 0.30 divider, 50 at 0.20 and at most 77 below, and its failed runs stall against the divider.

Why the divider alone cannot break it

The planner moves the car's centre, so the wall it must not cross is every centre position where the car overlaps the divider: the divider plus the car width, the red band in the scene. With a 0.13-wide car that band is never thinner than 0.13, and going from a 0.30 divider to 0.001 only shrinks it from 0.43 to 0.131. ntrl-demo resolves a band that wide. The thin dividers do leave a mark: the field's travel-time jump across the divider drops from 0.76–0.78 of the true jump to 0.61–0.64, and at the 0.01 and 0.005 dividers the downhill direction at 30–52 of 100 starts tips toward the wall, against none at 0.30. The band still stops the planner.

Halving the wall the field has to resolve

To keep halving that wall, the divider stays at 0.005 and the car gets narrower, which takes the C-space wall from 0.135 through 0.085, 0.055, 0.035 and 0.025 down to 0.015; each training seed's crossing was then bisected. Success holds at 99% or more down to 0.068 and is zero at 0.015 for every seed tested. In between, each trained field either resolves the wall or does not, and the training seed decides where: seed 2 falls to half near 0.047, seed 87358 near 0.027 (298 of 300 at 0.030, 150 at 0.027, 34 at 0.025), seed 1 near 0.022. The paths below show what the planner does as the car narrows: at width 0.13 every run backs out and loops round; at 0.02, 42 of the 50 shown get stuck at the divider; at 0.01 all 50 fail.

What fails is the field, not the planner

Below a 0.1 C-space wall, planning success follows how much of the true bay-to-bay travel time the field keeps (correlation 0.92 over 21 trained fields): fields that solve at least 200 of 300 runs keep 0.62–0.73 of it, fields below 100 keep 0.30–0.54. The profiles show where the time goes missing. Every field draws the wall: its travel time rises steeply into it and peaks at about the depth of the true ridge. What differs is where the far bay ends up. At the same 0.035 wall, the seed that plans 229 of 300 puts bay B at 0.58 and the seed that plans 7 puts it at 0.39, against a true 0.82; at 0.015 the field puts bay B no higher than the near side of the wall. ntrl-demo never supervises travel-time values: its speed label fixes how steep the field is, its normal label fixes the direction near walls (into the wall from both sides), and both are met by a field that rises into the wall and comes back down to any level beyond it. Only its weak temporal-difference term carries the cost of the route around. 99% of the failed runs touch the divider: 62% drive up to it and stall within 200 steps, the rest cut through. The oracle runs the same MPPI on the true travel time and solves 299–300 of 300 at every wall. A larger MPPI (200 samples, horizon 10, 400 steps) does not help; on thin walls it does worse, for example 113 against 229 of 300 at 0.035 for seed 87358.

Widening the car: narrow bays

The opposite test keeps both bays 0.23 wide (divider 0.01) and widens the car from 0.13 to 0.22, so the free space beside a parked car, the side gap, shrinks from 0.05 to 0.005 while the wall between the bays gets thicker. In ntrl-demo's speed model a gap under 0.033 slows the whole bay, and driving out of it costs 1/S(gap) per unit: a slope of 1.14 at a 0.025 gap, 2.8 at 0.0125, 18.5 at 0.005. ntrl-demo's own MPPI, with steps of 0.015, cannot get through such bays even on the true travel time (143 of 300 at 0.00625, 16 at 0.005), so the main planner here is the same MPPI with steps of 0.005 and 600 steps, which solves 300 of 300 on the true travel time at every gap. With it, a trained field falls to half success at a side gap of about 0.031 (seed 87358) and 0.022 (seed 1); seed 2 hovers near half from 0.035 to 0.025. Every seed fails at 0.0125 and below. That happens long before the slope gets steep: the bays need a slope of only 1.0–1.7 where the failures start, and at the tightest gaps the fields are steeper than required along the bay (24–46 against 10.7) but run the wrong way. In every failure the car slides sideways into the divider without backing out (a median of 0.000–0.065 of the 0.34 it has to reverse). At gaps of 0.0125 and below the field has no barrier at the divider: its travel time ramps straight across, pricing a crossing at 1.5–7 against a true 19, while driving around costs 7.7–13, so bay B is reached through the wall. At moderate gaps the line profiles can look right (seed 2 at a 0.018 gap) and the run still fails; what every field shares is a downhill direction at the start that leans toward the divider far more than the truth does (a median sideways share of 0.40–0.95 against 0.05–0.46), passing fields included. In a wide bay the field's rise near the wall stops that slide; in a narrow one there is no room. Below a gap of about 0.0045, ntrl-demo's speed model makes crossing the divider the true shortest route, so the sweep stops at 0.005.

Setup

  • Lot: the unit square with 0.02 outer walls; two bays (car width + 0.10 wide) opening toward −x at x = 0.10; car 0.30 × 0.13. Configuration (x, y, θ/2π) in ntrl-demo's box [−0.5, 0.5]³.
  • Clearance: exact signed distance between the car rectangle and the wall boxes, checked against brute force to 3·10⁻⁴ and against shapely's exact polygon distance to 10⁻⁶, including the labels the runs trained on. Speed label clip(d/margin, offset/margin, 1) with ntrl-demo's default margin 1/30; the trainer's stretch makes the slowest speed 0.012.
  • Data: ntrl-demo's point recipe in C-space (x0 near a wall, x1 up to √3 away), 500,000 pairs.
  • Training: ntrl-demo models/metric unchanged, through its own Model.train(): 5,000 epochs, about 7 minutes alone on either GPU.
  • Planner: ntrl-demo's MPPI from tests/arm_plan_stat.py (50 samples, horizon 5, up to 200 steps of 0.015, cost 10·T(first) + T(last)); the goal is appended to every path.
  • Success: converged and collision-free at every configuration along the path, interpolated at 0.001 or finer per coordinate. 100 queries × planning seeds 0, 1, 2 = 300 runs per trained field.
  • Truth: shortest paths on an (x, y, θ) grid with the same speed (0.005 in x and y, θ within ±43°), used for the oracle and the field diagnostics.
  • Widening sweep: bays fixed at 0.23 and divider 0.01 (so both bays' centre lines sit on truth-grid nodes); car widths 0.13 to 0.22. In bays tighter than 0.05 per side the parked poses vary by 0.3 of the gap in y and 0.3 of the tilt that closes it, and keep 0.3 of the gap as clearance. The small-step MPPI is ntrl-demo's MPPI with step 0.005 and 600 steps; both MPPIs were also run on the true travel time.

Caveats

  • Three training seeds for the ten main dividers and at C-space walls 0.135, 0.085, 0.055, 0.035, 0.030 and 0.025; two at 0.015; one at the other bisection points, the 0.002 and 0.001 dividers and for metric_arm. Near the threshold the seed decides the outcome, so a single-seed point there is a sample, not a rate.
  • Narrowing the car is how this test thins the C-space wall; with the car at 0.13 the divider alone cannot. Below roughly a 0.01 C-space wall, ntrl-demo's speed model (0.012 inside walls) makes cutting through nearly as cheap as driving around, so the test would stop measuring sharpness; it was not run.
  • θ is scaled as θ/2π without wrap-around, as the demo's arm package treats joints; the paths never rotate far.
  • Even where planning is perfect, the field's travel times sit 20–30% below the truth, and its speed correlates weakly with its own training labels on held-out pairs: it gets the travel-time structure right without fitting the local speed.
  • The widening sweep's main planner is not ntrl-demo's own MPPI, which fails in tight bays even on the truth; it is the same MPPI with a third of the step, which solves every query on the truth. On imperfect fields it is less forgiving than ntrl-demo's (seed 2 at the 0.05 control: 263 against 300 of 300).
  • Widening sweep: three training seeds at side gaps 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125, 0.00625 and 0.005, two at 0.035 and 0.018, one at 0.030 and 0.021. Why the fields lean toward the divider at moderate gaps is an interpretation consistent with the measurements, not a controlled finding.
